brief: You already trained today — Pull B, fifty-one minutes, logged this morning. So this card is for Legs B, and if you run it tomorrow that is three days in a row and your first leg night since 2 August. That gap is the single fact shaping the whole card. Start with what comes down. Smith RDL is three sets tonight, not four: 155 for eight, 185 for nine, 205 for nine — exactly your first three sets from 30 July. The 205 is untouched, because you have held it for eight, eight and nine across three Legs B nights and it is not a weight you are fighting. What comes off is the fourth exposure, and the reason is yesterday: you pulled four sets of Smith bent-over row and finished at 150 for ten, which is the same hinge and the same load on the lower back, twenty-four hours before this. This is a one-night call, not a change to the program — Legs B still asks for four sets next time. Four lifts go up, and every one of them is because of numbers you put in the log, not because a week went by. Leg press with your feet high runs at 180 for all three sets: on 30 July you finished 160 for twelve twice, which is the top of what that slot asks for on both sets, and then closed at 180 for ten. There is no pin between 160 and 180 on that machine, so re-printing 160 would hand you back a weight you have already maxed the reps on. The opener asks twelve because it comes fresh; the last set asks the ten you have already done there. Leg curl goes to 142.5. On 2 August you did 135 for fifteen and fifteen — Legs B only asks for ten to twelve, so fifteen is three reps past the ceiling, and 142.5 is one step on that machine. Calf press goes to 300 for twelve, three sets. You ran 280 for fifteen, fourteen and fifteen on 2 August; the leg press has no pin between 280 and 300, so the step is twenty pounds and the rep ask drops to twelve. Three sets, not four — that is the answer to the 'Why four sets' you wrote on 30 July, and it is the first Legs B since you asked. Cable crunch goes to 60 for twelve after a clean 55 for fifteen, fifteen, fifteen on 2 August; that machine moves in five-pound steps. Hanging leg raise holds at two sets of twelve, and it now asks REPS — the sixty-second version you swore at on 30 July is gone from the plan. Two cards are waiting on your plan screen and both take a tap. The first raises the hanging leg raise to twelve to fifteen reps on Legs B: there is no weight to add to that lift, twelve is the top of what it asks, and you have hit twelve three sittings running, so the slot is frozen and can never ask for more until the range moves. The second takes the Bulgarian split squat on Legs A from two sets to three. Be straight about that one: the program trainer wanted to hold it until two more Legs A nights are logged, which lands in September, and I put it on the card anyway rather than have it sit as words you cannot answer. Decline it if you disagree — that is a real answer and it closes the question. One thing nobody can fix with a card, handed to you rather than buried. Every core set you own is spinal flexion — six cable crunches and four leg raises a week — and there is nothing that resists rotation. The plank is the obvious answer and it is currently in no session at all: on 22 July you declined removing it, and a different card the same day swapped it out anyway. It cannot go back as things stand, for two reasons the program trainer checked himself: the exercise list has no anti-rotation movement in it, and the app's 'add' path cannot carry a seconds unit, so a plank added that way would print on your card as sixty REPS. That is the same bug that gave you the sixty-second leg raises. Nobody has fixed either in twenty-four days, and until one of them moves your core work stays one-directional. Last, unchanged: one bodyweight reading since January — 206 on 21 July — and one logged cardio session in the entire block. The scale is still the cheapest thing you can do for March.

proposals.why: The hanging leg raise carries no weight, so reps are the only thing about it that can ever grow — and the card asks you for your best set from last time, capped at the top of the range. On Legs B you did twelve and twelve, which is that cap, so this slot is now frozen at twelve and cannot ask for more no matter how easy it gets. Twelve to fifteen makes twelve the floor instead of the ceiling, and means a thirteen you take on your own sticks and becomes the new ask.

Legs A's split squat goes from two sets to three. It is the only single-leg work in your week and the smallest slot in the program, and you have finished both sets on every Legs A since it was added. The program trainer wanted to hold this until two more Legs A nights are logged, which puts it in September — I am putting it in front of you now instead, because a question you cannot answer is worse than one you decline.

overrides.reason: Three sets tonight, not four: 155 for eight, 185 for nine, 205 for nine — your first three sets from 30 July, with the top weight untouched. Yesterday you pulled four sets of Smith bent-over row and finished at 150 for ten, the same hinge and the same load on the lower back, twenty-four hours before this. The trainers split: one wanted all four sets with a tenth rep on each, and lost. Legs B still asks for four next time.

All three sets at 180. On 30 July you finished 160 for twelve twice — the top of what this slot asks for, on both sets — and then closed at 180 for ten. There is no pin between 160 and 180, so the choice was 180 or handing you back a weight you already maxed the reps on. The opener asks twelve because it comes fresh; the last set asks only the ten you have already done at 180.

142.5 for twelve, four sets. On 2 August you did 135 for fifteen and fifteen on Legs A. This slot only asks for ten to twelve, so fifteen is three reps past the ceiling and the weight has to move — 142.5 is one step on this machine, and it is the same number this card asked for on 30 July before you ran 135 instead.

300 for twelve, three sets. You ran 280 for fifteen, fourteen and fifteen on 2 August, which finishes that pin, and the leg press has nothing between 280 and 300 — so the step is twenty pounds and the rep ask drops to twelve. Three sets, not four: both trainers agreed on that, and it is the answer to the 'Why four sets' you wrote here on 30 July.

60 for twelve. On 2 August you did 55 for fifteen, fifteen and fifteen — the top of the range on every set, which is exactly when the weight moves. This machine steps in fives, so 60 is the next setting and the ask resets to twelve.

Two sets of twelve, unchanged, and both trainers agreed. Read the units once: this asks REPS, not seconds — the sixty-second version you objected to on 30 July came from the old plank slot and is gone from the plan. There is no weight to add here, which is why one of the cards on your plan screen asks to raise the rep range instead.

dissent.progression: Four sets at 155, 185, 205, 205 asking ten on every one — three sessions parked at 205 one rep short of the top of the range.
dissent.recovery: Three sets — 155 for eight, 185 for nine, 205 for nine — keeping the top load and dropping the fourth exposure after yesterday's rows.
dissent.why: Recovery, and this is the one lift where its private evidence decides it. He pulled four sets of Smith bent-over row finishing 150 for ten on 15 August: same hinge, same erector load, twenty-four hours before this session, and if Legs B lands tomorrow it is his third training day in a row and his first hinge in over two weeks. Progression's ask is not wrong on the record — it is asking for a tenth rep at 205 he has never taken, on the heaviest posterior lift in the program, on a re-entry night. Recovery keeps the 205 anyway, so nothing earned is given back. The fourth set is the cheapest thing on this card to spend.

dissent.progression: Retire 160 and run all three sets at 180 — he finished 160 for twelve twice, the top of the range on both.
dissent.recovery: Repeat 30 July exactly: 160, 160, 180, because the 180 set came in at ten, the floor of the range.
dissent.why: Progression. Recovery's case here is a reading of the load tables, which is not its slice and not its expertise — and it misses that the ten at 180 came last, after two sets at 160 he had already maxed the reps on. The fatigue argument recovery does own, I gave it in full on the RDL, which is the lift where spinal load and a third straight day actually bite. The leg press is machine-supported with no load on the back, 180 is the only pin above 160, and the card's last set asks only the ten he has already proved there.

dissent.progression: 142.5 for twelve on all four sets — 135 gave him fifteen twice on 2 August, three reps past this slot's ceiling.
dissent.recovery: Hold at 135, no load change on a first leg day back.
dissent.why: Progression, on evidence recovery cannot see. The 2 August Legs A session is the newest leg-curl data in the log and it is decisive: fifteen reps at a weight whose slot asks for ten to twelve means the pin is provably light, and 142.5 is a single step. Recovery's own reason for holding was that it had already cut a Smith RDL set and did not want to take hamstring volume down twice — that argues for keeping four sets, which this does. The load is the part it had no evidence against.

dissent.progression: 300 for twelve, three sets — 280 is finished after fifteen, fourteen, fifteen on 2 August.
dissent.recovery: 260 for fifteen then 280 for thirteen twice — the first three sets of 30 July, three sets not four.
dissent.why: Progression on the load, and the seats already agreed on the thing that matters most here, which is three sets rather than four. Recovery's numbers would ask him for less than he actually did on 2 August — 280 for fifteen, fourteen and fifteen — which is a step backwards dressed as caution, and it happens because recovery is reading a 30 July session while newer and better work sits in the log. The leg press has no pin between 280 and 300, so twenty pounds is the only step available, and the rep ask drops from fifteen to twelve to pay for it.

dissent.progression: 60 for twelve after a clean sweep of 55 for fifteen, fifteen, fifteen on 2 August.
dissent.recovery: Hold at 55 — the load is not in question and the slot costs almost nothing, so leave it.
dissent.why: Progression. Both seats read the same lift as low-cost and low-risk; the difference is that one of them noticed he took every set to the top of the range twelve days ago, which is the exact condition for the weight to move. Holding a finisher he has swept is how a slot sits still for a month. Five pounds on an ab machine is not a risk anyone at this table argued against.
